2026-11-01|ls-assigned-land: Assigned land: why it cannot be sold and what the law says Land School · source: “Assigned Land in India: Why It Cannot Be Sold and What the Law Says” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Assigned land = government surplus/wasteland granted to landless poor families for cultivation or house sites — possession and use, NOT free ownership. Transfers are prohibited or void under state land-reform laws; a registered sale deed changes nothing. The government can RESUME the land at any time, with no compensation to the buyer — and buying it can carry up to six months’ jail. Narrow exceptions: inheritance by heirs, bank mortgages, and good-faith pre-Act purchases by landless poor persons. The whole defence is two checks: the revenue record’s remarks and the Section 22-A prohibited list. What assigned land is Government surplus or wasteland handed to landless poor persons — typically agricultural labourers or SC/ST families — for cultivation or as a house site, under land-reform and welfare schemes. What transfers is possession and limited use rights; ownership stays CONDITIONAL with the state. The condition that matters to every buyer: the grant usually prohibits sale. Why the law bans its sale The point of assignment is welfare — land in the hands of the landless. If assignees could sell, the poor would be bought out for quick cash and the policy would defeat itself; so state laws (in Telangana, the Assigned Lands (Prohibition of Transfers) Act) bar selling, gifting, leasing or otherwise transferring without government permission, and declare violating transfers invalid. What “void ab initio” means Treated as if the transaction never legally happened — no title passes, ever. Even land that changed hands TEN times through ten registered deeds: every link is equally invalid. A registered document does not make you the owner here; the paper has no legal weight at all. One narrow protection exists: a landless poor person who bought in good faith, for value, from the original assignee BEFORE the Act commenced and was in possession on that date — it protects the poor, not an investor. Definition — Void ab initio: void “from the beginning” — not cancelled later, but never valid at any moment. Nothing downstream of it can be valid either. What happens if it is sold anyway The government can resume the land at ANY time — no limitation period runs in its favour going away — and reassign it to another eligible landless family. The buyer gets no compensation; no civil court can decree the sale into existence. And the consequence sellers never mention: acquiring assigned land in breach of the prohibition is an OFFENCE carrying up to six months’ imprisonment. The buyer is not just a victim in this law’s eyes. Transferability by land category Category Freely transferable? Notes Patta (private) land Yes Ordinary sale deed + registration Assigned land No Transfer void; resumption + penal risk Tribal-area land Highly restricted Transfers to non-tribals barred in scheduled areas Ceiling-surplus land No Vested in government for redistribution Endowment (temple) land No Alienation needs statutory sanction, rarely given Forest land No Central law bars de-reservation without approval What an assignee CAN do Cultivate for the family; pass the land to legal heirs (inheritance is generally not a prohibited transfer); mortgage it to a scheduled bank, co-operative or notified institution — the one security the Act permits; build a house where the assignment was a house site. And in some states, apply to the Collector for DE-RESTRICTION — converting it into regular patta land eligible for sale once eligibility conditions are met. Rules vary; the revenue authority’s word is the only one that counts. How to check whether a plot is assigned Pull the latest Record of Rights from the state revenue department and read the REMARKS column for “assigned”, “granted” or restriction notes. Check the state’s prohibited-property register (Section 22-A list) for the survey number. Ask the local revenue office directly. And read the original ASSIGNMENT ORDER — it states plainly whether transfer is prohibited. Fifteen minutes of record-reading is the difference between owning land and owning a legal dead end. Example: The classic Hyderabad-belt trap: a corridor plot at 40% below market, seller waving a registered deed from a 2009 purchase. The RoR remarks column reads “asgd”. That deed — and the one before it — are both void; the discount was the disclosure. Walk away; no lawyer can cure it. If you are the assignee wanting to sell Apply to the competent revenue authority for removal of the transfer restriction where state law permits, BEFORE entering any agreement. For SC/ST or tribal-origin land, confirm whether Collector approval is mandatory. Selling first and regularising later is not a sequence the law recognises. Quick answers (FAQ) Can assigned land be sold after N years? No automatic ripening — only formal de-restriction changes its status. Why do registered deeds exist on assigned land? Because registration only blocks parcels actually on the prohibited list; the registrar’s stamp never validates a void transfer. Can family inherit it? Yes — heirs succeed; that is not a prohibited transfer. Can it be mortgaged? Only to banks/institutions the Act permits. Can it ever become freehold? In some states, via Collector-approved conversion to patta land. Bottom line Assigned land is the one category where late homework has NO remedy — no cure, no compensation, no sympathetic court. The RoR remarks and the 22-A list, checked before any money moves, are the entire safeguard. For you: For a plotting developer this is the first gate on every parcel — before price, before layout dreams: Dharani/RoR remarks + 22-A check on each survey number. One assigned survey number inside an assembled venture can poison the whole layout’s marketability. Make the check a fixed line item in your acquisition template. Glossary — every term, simply SIR (Special Intensive Revision) A nationwide exercise by the Election Commission to re-check and rebuild electoral rolls from scratch, intended to remove duplicate, dead or ineligible voters. Example: it is similar in spirit to a housing society re-verifying every resident’s name against ID proof before printing a new register — necessary in principle, but capable of wrongly dropping a real resident if the verification is rushed or poorly targeted. CEC (Chief Election Commissioner) The head of the three-member Election Commission of India, appointed by the President on the government’s recommendation (under a process set by a 2023 law), and removable only through a judicial-impeachment-style process. Example: comparable in insulation from everyday political pressure to a Supreme Court judge, at least on paper. Electoral roll The official list of everyone registered to vote in a given constituency; being removed from it means being unable to vote there even if otherwise eligible. Example: like being removed from a building’s resident register — you can still live there, but you can’t vote in the society’s elections until you’re re-added. ‘Vote chori’ (vote theft) A political slogan, not a legal term, used by the opposition INDIA bloc to describe what it alleges is systematic, deliberate removal of genuine voters (rather than honest clean-up of duplicate or dead entries) that benefits the ruling party. Example: the term functions like “scam” in Indian political shorthand — a label applied before, not after, any formal finding. Vanara sena / Ravana (Ramayana reference) In the Hindu epic Ramayana, Lord Rama’s army of monkey-warriors (the “vanara sena”), led by Hanuman, helps him defeat the ten-headed demon king Ravana and rescue his wife Sita. Example: Indian politicians very commonly borrow this story's good-versus-evil structure to cast their own side as Rama’s army and a rival as Ravana — it is rhetorical costume, not a claim about facts. INDIA bloc Short for the opposition alliance formed in 2023 to jointly contest the ruling BJP-led NDA (National Democratic Alliance); includes Congress and multiple regional parties that otherwise often compete against each other in their own states. Example: like rival cricket franchises temporarily fielding a combined XI against one shared opponent. Ramlila Maidan A large public ground in central Delhi historically used for staging the biggest political rallies in Indian politics, including some that have helped topple national governments. Example: its symbolic weight is similar to a political party choosing to hold its biggest rally at a city’s most historically significant public square rather than any ordinary stadium. TPCC (Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee) The Congress party's formal state-level organisational unit for Telangana, headed in this story by B. Mahesh Kumar Goud. Example: functions like a state branch office of a national company, with its own local head answerable to the national headquarters. South Central Railway (SCR) / Railway zone Indian Railways is divided into zones for operational management; SCR covers Telangana and parts of neighbouring states and answers to the central Railway Board, not any state government. Example: like a regional branch of a nationally-owned utility company — locally present, but centrally controlled. Article 324 of the Constitution The constitutional provision establishing the Election Commission of India and setting out the (judicial-impeachment-style) process for removing a Chief Election Commissioner. Example: the same basic design logic as the protection given to Supreme Court judges — meant to keep the officer insulated from ordinary political pressure. 4. Tue, 27 Oct 2026 South Central Railway declines Telangana Congress’s request for five special trains to carry roughly 15,000 workers to the planned 1 November Delhi rally. Wed, 28 Oct 2026 Telangana Congress workers protest outside SCR headquarters in Secunderabad; police detain some protesters. The party pivots to arranging roughly 150–200 private buses instead. Sun, 1 Nov 2026 The INDIA bloc’s “Vote Bachao, Desh Bachao” rally is held at Ramlila Maidan, Delhi. Rahul Gandhi, Kharge, Mamata Banerjee, Akhilesh Yadav and Revanth Reddy all speak; Revanth Reddy makes the “vanara sena”/“Ravana” remark; BJP calls it “disgraceful” and disputes turnout. The deeper forces at work here run well beyond one rally. Disputes over the accuracy and fairness of India’s electoral rolls are not new — similar flashpoints have recurred around National Register of Citizens debates in Assam and West Bengal, and around state-specific roll revisions in Bihar earlier in the SIR cycle. What is specific to this moment is the scale of the claimed deletions (13-plus crore names, if the opposition’s figure holds up) landing in the run-up to a dense multi-state election calendar, which raises the stakes of any roll dispute far above a routine administrative housekeeping exercise. A ten-year follower of Indian politics would also recognise the Ramayana-framing device itself as a well-worn tool — Indian politicians across the spectrum have cast rivals as various mythological villains for decades — and would read Revanth Reddy’s remark less as news in itself and more as a data point on how combative Telangana’s Congress leadership is willing to be on the national stage, which is the more durable signal for Vivek to track. 5. So what — stakes and consequences The rally and the remark both serve fairly narrow, short-term purposes for each side. Revanth Reddy and Telangana Congress gain visibility and base-energising theatre at minimal real cost — a sharp quote costs nothing administratively. The BJP gains a clean, quotable “disgraceful” counter-line and a turnout dispute that lets it avoid engaging with the underlying SIR deletion numbers directly. The Election Commission, notably, said nothing in any source found in this edition’s research — it is the subject of the rally, not a participant in the day’s exchange of quotes. Watch: (a) whether the Election Commission or CEC Gyanesh Kumar's office issues any formal response to the resignation demand (moderate likelihood of a terse statement, low likelihood of any actual resignation); (b) whether SIR-related deletion disputes surface specifically in Telangana or Hyderabad in the coming weeks, given a separate (pre-window) report of steep Hyderabad voter-roll cuts under SIR; (c) whether the Miyapur land-auction Cabinet decision slips further while the Chief Minister’s public bandwidth stays focused on national rallies (plausible, unconfirmed); (d) whether the Railways-Congress train dispute recurs ahead of any future Delhi mobilisation. What this means for you: (a) For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically: nothing here changes any title, approval or auction directly, but a Chief Minister and ruling party visibly consumed by national political combat is a soft signal that administratively heavy decisions sitting with his Cabinet — the Miyapur auction foremost among them — may move slower than the political announcements around them suggest. Price that lag into any plan that assumes a near-term Miyapur auction. (b) For business and investment generally: voter-roll disputes at this scale are a leading indicator of how contested the next election cycle will be, which tends to correlate with how much a ruling party leans on populist land/resource announcements (free land for the poor, auction proceeds to welfare schemes) rather than steady administrative process in the run-up to polls. The beginner’s mistake is to read this story as pure noise with zero relevance to a plotting developer's business and skip it entirely. The sharper, expert read is narrower but real: this is a bandwidth and tempo signal, not a land-policy signal — it tells you how to pace your own expectations of government decision-making speed this month, not what any decision will be. 6. The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map Telangana's Congress Chief Minister used a mythological insult against the Prime Minister at a huge opposition rally in Delhi, protesting a national voter-roll exercise his own party says has wrongly deleted over 13 crore names; his own party's workers got there by bus after the Railways refused them special trains, which both sides read through their own political lens. None of it changes a single land record, approval or rupee in Telangana today. What it changes is where the state's top political attention is currently pointed — toward Delhi and national electoral combat, not toward the Cabinet decisions on land sitting in Hyderabad. 2026-11-02|ls-capital-gains: Capital gains tax on agricultural land sale Land School · source: “Capital Gains Tax on Agricultural Land Sale in India” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Rural agricultural land is NOT a capital asset under Section 2(14)(iii) — its sale attracts no capital gains tax at all. The rural test is mechanical: the nearest municipality’s census population, and aerial distance of 2 / 6 / 8 km. Urban agricultural land is taxed like any property; long-term starts at 24 months. Section 54B exemption needs TWO years of actual farming before sale, reinvestment in farmland within two years, and a three-year lock-in on the new land. Section 50C lets the taxman substitute the stamp-duty value when you sell below it. When the tax applies at all One question decides everything: is the land RURAL or URBAN under the Income Tax Act? Rural agricultural land is excluded from the very definition of a capital asset by Section 2(14)(iii) — no capital asset, no capital gain, nothing to tax. Urban agricultural land gets no carve-out and is taxed like any other asset. Two owners can sell what looks like the same plot and one pays nothing while the other owes tax on the whole gain — purely because of where the land sits. The rural test — mechanical, not agricultural Nothing to do with how the land is farmed; everything to do with location and population. Land is RURAL if it lies outside a municipality or cantonment of 10,000+ people, AND outside these aerial distances from those limits: 2 km where the population is 10,000–1 lakh; 6 km where it is 1–10 lakh; 8 km where it exceeds 10 lakh. Population comes from the last published census; distance is measured AERIALLY — as the crow flies, not as the road winds. Inside the limits = urban agricultural land = taxable. One nuance: the exemption attaches to the LAND — a farmhouse, well or standing trees sold in the same deal are valued and treated separately. Example: Two farmers sell near Hyderabad (population >10 lakh, so the 8 km band applies). One’s land sits 9 km aerially from the municipal limit — rural, gain fully exempt. The other’s sits 7 km out — urban, fully taxable. Same crop, same buyer profile, two kilometres of geometry worth lakhs in tax. The second test: was it actually farmed? Classification decides the tax; CULTIVATION decides whether your claim survives scrutiny. Revenue records carry seasonal cultivation entries — the evidence that agricultural operations actually happened — and Section 54B leans on exactly that record for its two-year farming condition. Land held bare as pure investment is where exemption claims die at assessment. How the gain is computed Sale price minus purchase cost and expenses. Held 24+ months: long-term. The current long-term regime taxes gains at 12.5% without indexation (indexation having been withdrawn for post-July-2024 sales). And Section 50C looms over the price itself: sell below the stamp-duty value and the department can treat THAT value as your deemed sale price, subject to a tolerance margin — the guideline value quietly setting your tax floor. Rural vs urban at a glance Aspect Rural agricultural land Urban agricultural land Capital asset? No — s.2(14)(iii) excludes it Yes Capital gains tax None LTCG/STCG as applicable TDS on sale (194-IA) Expressly excluded 1% at ₹50 lakh+ (resident seller) Exemption routes Not needed 54B (farmland), 54EC (bonds) The exits: 54B and 54EC Section 54B — individuals and HUFs: reinvest the gain in NEW agricultural land within two years, provided the sold land was farmed for the two years before sale; money not yet reinvested by the return-filing date parks in a Capital Gains Account Scheme; the new land locks in for three years — sell early and the exemption unwinds. Section 54EC — the alternative for long-term gains: NHAI/REC/PFC/IRFC bonds within six months (₹50 lakh cap, five-year lock). The taxes that ride alongside TDS: buyers deduct 1% under 194-IA on urban agricultural land at ₹50 lakh+ — rural land is expressly outside the section. NRI sellers: Section 195 instead, at much higher rates — plan with a lower-deduction certificate. 50C: as above, the stamp-value floor. Quick answers (FAQ) Is rural agricultural land exempt? Fully — it is not a capital asset. How is “rural” defined? The census-population + aerial-distance test above. Indexation still available? Not under the current 12.5% regime. Urban land exemptions? 54B with the farming and lock-in conditions; 54EC bonds. TDS on farmland? Urban yes (₹50L+), rural no. Don’t want to buy farmland again? 54EC bonds, or pay the 12.5% and stay liquid. Bottom line Before selling any farmland, establish three things in writing: the aerial distance to the nearest 10,000+ municipality, the census figure that sets the band, and the cultivation record. Those three lines decide whether the tax is zero, exempt-with-conditions, or fully payable — get a CA’s letter where kilometres decide lakhs. For you: For your JD landowner partners this is THE conversation: many Ranga Reddy parcels sit inside Hyderabad’s 8 km band — urban, taxable — while one village further out is exempt. Knowing which side of the line a family’s land falls (and flagging 54B’s two-year farming condition early) makes you the developer who saved them lakhs before the deal even signed. 2026-11-02|ls-mutation: Mutation of land records: what it is and why it matters Land School · source: “Mutation of Land Records: What It Is and Why It Matters” by 1acre.in Key Highlights Mutation updates the owner’s name in the government’s revenue register after sale, inheritance, gift or partition — it does NOT transfer ownership; registration did that. Skipping it is a top reason buyers fight tax notices and loan rejections years after a purchase. The name changes by state — dakhil kharij, intiqal, patta transfer, khata transfer — the process is the same. A DISPUTED claim cannot be mutated by a revenue officer: it goes to civil court first. The Supreme Court’s position cuts both ways: mutation is not proof of title — but its ABSENCE is proof something was never finished. What mutation is The update of the government’s revenue register to show the CURRENT owner’s name after a sale, inheritance, gift or partition. It is different from the sale deed and registration: mutation affects the tax and revenue record and does not by itself prove legal title. Rural land mutates at the revenue office; urban property at the municipal corporation. The application typically needs the sale deed, previous mutation records and identity proof — and it matters for paying property tax under the right name, and for every future loan or resale. Definition — Mutation (dakhil kharij / khata transfer / patta transfer): the state updating its own ledger of who holds the land — the bridge between the registered deed and the revenue record. Registration changes OWNERSHIP; mutation changes the government’s BOOKS. What the process verifies Not a rubber stamp. The reviewing officer checks that the applicant is the rightful new owner based on a valid transfer document — sale deed, gift deed, or inheritance record — and cross-checks the property’s survey number, area and boundaries against the existing revenue record. What the exercise CANNOT do: establish or guarantee title. It aligns the ledger; it does not adjudicate ownership — which is why a disputed claim goes to civil court, not the Tehsildar. Documents by route How the land came to you Core document for mutation Purchase Registered sale deed Gift Registered gift deed Inheritance (no will) Death certificate + legal-heir certificate Inheritance (will) Death certificate + will (probate where applicable) Partition Registered partition deed / decree Most state portals also want the latest tax receipt and identity proof, whatever the route. One heir applying while others exist? Expect to produce their no-objection letters and an indemnity bond. Why it matters An unmutated register keeps showing the OLD owner though the sale is legally complete. Consequences compound: tax bills keep going to the previous owner while unpaid dues attach to the LAND, not the person; banks reject loans because mutation status is a basic ownership check; resale gets harder because the next buyer’s advocate flags the mismatch instantly; and heir disputes drag for years while land sits under a deceased owner’s name. Example: A buyer purchases in 2018, never mutates. In 2024 a tax-arrears notice arrives — the previous owner’s unpaid dues, now attached to the land. Then the bank declines a mortgage: “record shows a different owner”. Two problems, one skipped application that would have taken a few weeks in 2018. When to apply Immediately after any transaction — some states now run online or even automated mutation for straightforward transfers, others still take manual applications at the revenue office. The two classic delays: assuming the sale deed alone is enough, and inherited land sitting unmutated across a generation. Buying land that moved informally within a family? Ask whether mutation was completed at EACH step, not just the latest. Buying? Check mutation status first The seller-vs-record match is precisely the check that fails on an unmutated parcel — and it is checkable from outside (Dharani in Telangana shows the current pattadar). A mismatch does not always mean fraud; it always means an unfinished step someone must complete before your money moves. Quick answers (FAQ) Does mutation transfer ownership? No — registration does; mutation records it. How long does it take? Weeks for clean files; longer with objections. Can I sell unmutated land? Legally the registered owner can — practically, buyers and their banks balk; mutate first. Heir dispute during mutation? The revenue officer steps aside; civil court decides. Need a lawyer? Not for a clean application; yes the moment there is an objection. Mandatory for agricultural land? Effectively yes — the revenue record drives everything from tax to crop entries. Does it affect loans? Directly — lenders treat it as a gating check. Bottom line Easy to postpone, expensive to ignore. Mutation keeps your name accurate in the records that decide your tax bill, your loan eligibility and your next sale — apply promptly, and when buying, treat the seller’s mutation status as part of the title check. For you: Build it into your buyer experience: hand every plot purchaser a mutation-application pack at registration (or file it for them). Ventures whose buyers’ records are clean resell faster — and resales are your best advertising. On the acquisition side: an unmutated seller is a seller who cannot close on your timeline; surface it in week one, not at the SRO.
